headline: Robinson's Hole loaded with peanuts, bass and blues eating good — albies still a no-show
subhead: The bait is exactly where it should be and the water's crossed the mark, but the first albie of the season hasn't shown its tail yet in Buzzards Bay or the Vineyard rips.
body_markdown:
Stood on the rocks at Robinson's Hole Tuesday evening watching peanut bunker ball up so tight against the current seam they looked like a shadow moving under the surface. Silversides doing the same thing over at Quick's Hole, pinned against the west side current line on the last two hours of the ebb. That's the tell. That's the bait signature we watch for every single year right before the first albie shows, and right now it's checking every box except the one that matters — I haven't had a confirmed albie or bonito report cross my desk yet out of this corridor. Close. Not there.

We flagged this corridor as one of the hottest early-arrival zones on the coastwide watch last week, and the setup hasn't backed off one bit. Water's pushed well past the seasonal threshold everywhere from Woods Hole down through the Elizabeths, the tide is still carrying push from the full moon, and it's building again toward the August 12 new moon. That's the exact recipe — warm water, hard current, bait getting squeezed through the rips. It's a matter of days, not weeks, but I'm not going to tell you the fish are here when they're not. Anyone telling you they boated an albie in Buzzards Bay this week ahead of me is either mistaken or fishing a different ocean.

What IS biting, and biting well, is the interim program that always carries us into the albie window. Striped bass are stacked on the west side of Cuttyhunk and along the backside of Nashawena, working the rips on the last of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming — that current-change window is money right now. Bass in the mid-20s to low 30-inch class, some better fish mixed in after dark, eating swimming plugs and 1.5-ounce bucktails with white or chartreuse tails bounced right off the rip edge where the sand gives way to cobble. Bluefish are thick through the same water, chopping bait on top hard enough that you can hear it from the boat before you see it — poppers and single-hook Deadly Dicks worked fast across the slicks have been producing non-stop action, though these blues will fray you off if you're running mono leader, so step up to 40-pound fluoro minimum.

Fluke are holding to the script too — steady rather than spectacular, which is exactly how I'd describe it to a buddy who asked me straight. Drifting the drop-off outside Tarpaulin Cove and the deeper edges around Quick's Hole in 25 to 35 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with squid strips, dragged slow on the moving tide. Keepers mixed with a lot of shorts — you're working for your five fish, not filling a cooler in an hour, but the quality fish are there if you cover water and stay on structure edges rather than open sand.

Scup fishing has been the easy win all week, and honestly it's a good way to keep the rod bent while you're waiting on bigger things to show. Squid strips and sandworms on double-hook bottom rigs around the Woods Hole draw bridge pilings and the rocky structure off Nonamesset are producing steady action, good eating-size fish, no drama, just consistent bites on the bottom during the tide change.

Here's how I'm reading the next stretch. The bait's doing exactly what it should — balling tight in the rips, getting pinned by current, sitting right where albies and bonito want to find it when they push through. Water temps have crossed the mark across the whole regional watch, from Montauk up through here, and the tide's building back toward that mid-August new moon push. If I had to put money on a spot for the first fish, I'd watch Robinson's Hole and Menemsha basin hardest — both have deep, fast current lines right against structure, which is exactly the setup albies use to pin bait when they arrive. Gay Head's rip is the other one I'd keep an eye on; when the tide runs hard there on a clean afternoon with light wind, that's historically been ground zero for the first scout fish of the season.

My plan for the coming week is simple — keep the light spinning gear rigged with small epoxy jigs and Deadly Dicks in the rocket launcher, fish the bass and blues on the rip changes like I have been, and check the bait balls at first light and last light every single day. That's when the first albie tail usually shows, a quick slash through a bait pod that's gone before you can even get a cast off. If a stretch of calm, sunny days holds through the weekend and that tide keeps building, I would not be surprised to hear the first credible report out of this water within the next week to ten days. Until then, the bass and blues are worth the trip on their own, and the fluke and scup will keep you occupied between rip changes. Just don't put the epoxy jigs away yet.
